newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt to retain minimum intervention role - Tsang.
newsitem.headline: HK govt to retain minimum intervention role - Tsang.

text.p: Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said on Wednesday that the Hong Kong government will continue to follow a policy of minimum intervention in the economy after the handover.

"We will continue doing exactly what we were doing before in the sense that we will make sure that the government will continue to provide the most efficient infrastructure for this place," Tsang told Reuters in an interview.

"Our philosophy will remain the same in that economic growth is guided by the market and will be led by businessmen. The role of government must be to continue to provide infrastructure -- the telecommunications, the roads, the airport and the human resources."
Tsang said he believed Hong Kong's hands-off policy was one of the fundamental reasons why the territory has been successful.
The policy also is enshrined in the Basic Law, Hong Kong's constitution after it reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, he said.
"Our industrial policy in my view is part and parcel of what is guaranteed in the Basic Law in that we are not going to change our fundamental economic system in Hong Kong," he said.

Some members of the incoming Executive Council, the group of advisers positioned between future leader Tung Chee-hwa and the legislation, argue in favour of the development of a high technology sector in Hong Kong.
Other economic commentators object to any suggestion of government intervention in Hong Kong's economy, which has thrived under a laissez-faire management policy.
As financial secretary, the second most powerful bureaucrat in executive-led Hong Kong, Tsang also sits on the Executive Council.
"As financial secretary, I have always been under pressure to change things, to shell out more money for pork-barrelling politics, for subsidising industry, for subsidising transport," he said.

"I have a pretty tough skin on this. I know (where) Hong Kong's longer term interests lie, in my view, and I think we have got international bodies supporting my views and the local community generally agrees with me, too."
